QuestionText: Electric current is the flow of ___
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Electric current is defined as the flow of electric charge (electrons) through a conductor.

QuestionText: The SI unit of electric current is
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: The SI unit of electric current is the Ampere (A), measured using an ammeter.

QuestionText: The device used to measure electric current is
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: An ammeter measures the electric current flowing in a circuit; it is connected in series.

QuestionText: The potential difference (voltage) in a circuit is measured by a
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: A voltmeter measures the potential difference (voltage) between two points; connected in parallel.

QuestionText: A device that breaks or completes an electric circuit is called a
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: A switch controls the flow of current by opening (breaking) or closing (completing) the circuit.

QuestionText: Materials that allow electric current to pass through them are called
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Conductors have free electrons that allow electric current to flow through them (e.g. copper, iron).

QuestionText: Materials that do not allow electric current to pass through are called
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Insulators have tightly bound electrons and do not allow current flow (e.g. rubber, plastic, wood).

QuestionText: Which of the following is a good conductor of electricity?
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Copper is a metal with free electrons and is an excellent conductor of electricity.

QuestionText: The heating effect of electric current is used in
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: When current flows through a resistance, heat is generated (Joule's heating): used in heaters, toasters, and bulbs.

QuestionText: The filament of an electric bulb is made of ___
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Tungsten has a very high melting point (~3422 degrees C) and high resistance, making it ideal for bulb filaments.

QuestionText: A fuse wire is used to ___
Options: A) Protect the circuit from excessive current (short circuit)
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: A fuse melts when current exceeds safe limits, breaking the circuit and protecting appliances from damage.

QuestionText: Which material is used for fuse wire?
Options: A) Alloy of tin and lead (low melting point)
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Fuse wire is made from tin-lead alloy (or other low-melting-point metals) that melt quickly at excess current.

QuestionText: The magnetic effect of electric current was discovered by
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Oersted discovered in 1820 that an electric current creates a magnetic field around it.

QuestionText: When electric current passes through a coil of wire wound around an iron core, it acts as a
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: An electromagnet is a coil of wire carrying current wrapped around a soft iron core; it behaves as a magnet.

QuestionText: An electromagnet loses its magnetism when
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Electromagnets are temporary: they only act as magnets while current flows through the coil.

QuestionText: Which of these uses the heating effect of electric current?
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Electric iron converts electrical energy to heat using the heating effect of current.

QuestionText: An electric bell uses the ___ of electric current
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: An electric bell uses an electromagnet (magnetic effect) to attract and release the striker to ring the bell.

QuestionText: A circuit in which all components are connected end-to-end in a single path is called
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: In a series circuit, components are connected in a single loop; same current flows through all.

QuestionText: In a series circuit if one bulb fuses
Options: A) All other bulbs also go off
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Series circuit has only one path; if one component fails (breaks), the entire circuit opens and all go off.

QuestionText: In a parallel circuit if one bulb fuses
Options: A) Other bulbs continue to glow
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Parallel circuits have multiple paths; if one branch fails, other branches remain complete and functional.

QuestionText: Household wiring uses ___ circuit
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Household wiring uses parallel circuits so each appliance gets the same voltage and operates independently.

QuestionText: A short circuit is dangerous because
Options: A) It causes very high current and fire
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: A short circuit creates a low-resistance path: very high current flows, generating heat and potential fire.

QuestionText: The strength of an electromagnet can be increased by
Options: A) Increasing current or number of turns in coil
C) Using a smaller iron core
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Electromagnet strength depends on: current strength, number of turns, and core material. More turns or higher current = stronger magnet.

QuestionText: The symbol for a battery in a circuit diagram consists of
Options: A) Long and short alternating lines (cells in series)
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Battery symbol: alternating long (positive) and short (negative) lines representing cells connected in series.

QuestionText: Which effect of current is used in electroplating?
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Electroplating uses the chemical (electrolytic) effect of electric current to deposit a metal layer.

QuestionText: What happens to the resistance of a metallic conductor when its temperature increases?
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: For metallic conductors, resistance increases with temperature due to increased atomic vibrations.

QuestionText: LED stands for
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: LED (Light Emitting Diode) converts electrical energy directly into light; more efficient than incandescent bulbs.

QuestionText: Which is more energy efficient?
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: LED bulbs are most energy efficient: they convert most electricity directly to light with minimal heat loss.

QuestionText: MCB stands for
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: An MCB (Miniature Circuit Breaker) is a safety device that automatically trips when current exceeds safe levels; modern replacement for fuses.

QuestionText: Electric energy is measured in
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Electrical energy consumed is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh) or units. 1 unit = 1 kWh.

QuestionText: Power consumed by an appliance is calculated as
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Power = Voltage × Current (P = VI). SI unit: Watt (W).

QuestionText: An appliance of 1000 W is used for 2 hours. Energy consumed in units (kWh) is
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Energy = Power × Time = 1 kW × 2 h = 2 kWh (2 units).

QuestionText: The effect of current that makes a compass needle deflect is
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Oersted showed that current produces a magnetic field, which deflects a nearby compass needle.

QuestionText: Resistance of a conductor depends on
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Resistance R = ρL/A, where ρ is resistivity (material property), L is length, and A is cross-sectional area.

QuestionText: If resistance of a wire is doubled (by doubling length) and voltage is same, the current
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: V = IR. If R doubles and V is constant: I = V/R = V/2R = half the original current.

QuestionText: Which of these is an application of the magnetic effect of current?
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Electric motors use the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field to produce rotation.

QuestionText: Thick copper wire is used for household wiring because thick wire has
Options: A) Lower resistance and carries high current safely
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Thicker wire has larger cross-section, lower resistance, carries more current without excessive heating.

QuestionText: The purpose of earthing (grounding) in electrical wiring is to
Options: A) Provide safe path for leakage current to Earth
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Earthing provides a safe low-resistance path to ground for any fault current, preventing electric shock.

QuestionText: What colour is the earth wire in Indian electrical systems?
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Earth wire in India: green or yellow-green. Live: red/brown. Neutral: black/blue.

QuestionText: An electric heater draws 5 A at 220 V. Its power is
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects

QuestionText: Three bulbs 60W, 100W, and 40W connected in parallel to 220V. Which draws the most current?
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: P=VI so I=P/V. Higher power = higher current at same voltage. 100W draws most current.

QuestionText: The resistance of a 100W, 220V bulb is approximately
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects

QuestionText: Why is tungsten used for bulb filament and not copper?
Options: A) Tungsten has very high melting point and high resistivity
D) Copper melts at room temperature
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Tungsten's very high melting point (3422 C) allows it to operate at white-hot temperatures without melting.

QuestionText: In an electromagnet increasing number of turns while keeping current constant will
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: More turns means more magnetic field lines: stronger electromagnet for the same current.

QuestionText: Two resistors 4 Ω and 6 Ω in series across 10V. Current in circuit is
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects

QuestionText: What is the voltage across the 4 Ω resistor in the above question?
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects

QuestionText: A fuse of 5A rating is used in a circuit. If current exceeds 5A the fuse
Options: A) Melts and breaks the circuit
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: The fuse wire melts when current exceeds its rated value, breaking the circuit and preventing damage.

QuestionText: Which of these is a correct safety practice with electricity?
Options: A) Never touch electrical appliances with wet hands
B) Use bare wire without insulation
C) Overload one socket with many plugs
D) Touch wires to test if live
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Water conducts electricity: touching live appliances with wet hands risks fatal electric shock.

QuestionText: Voltage (potential difference) is measured in
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Potential difference is measured in Volts (V) using a voltmeter.

QuestionText: Nichrome is used as heating element in electric heaters because it
Options: A) Has high resistance and high melting point
Topic: Physics - Electric Current and Its Effects
Explanation: Nichrome (nickel-chromium alloy) has high resistivity and melting point, producing substantial heat without melting.
